newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel cabinet sidesteps decision on savings tax.
newsitem.headline: Israel cabinet sidesteps decision on savings tax.

text.p: Israel's cabinet sidestepped on Monday a decision on a politically sensitive tax on short-term savings, adopting only part of the finance ministry's proposed capital market reform package, officials said.
The short-term savings tax was the key component of the reform, which aims to encourage long-term savings and boost the ailing stock and bond markets.

"Senior officials on the level of directors-general from the Bank of Israel, the finance ministry, and the prime minister's office will continue to debate the savings tax issue for two weeks," a finance ministry spokeswoman told Reuters.
"Until then, no tax will be implemented."
Treasury sources said Finance Minister Dan Meridor was opposed to the compromise decision, reached after a marathon meeting of the cabinet that lasted into the pre-dawn hours on Monday.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who took office last June with a promise not to raise taxes, led the cabinet majority in favour of the compromise.
The spokeswoman said the two-week delay would also apply to a range of other measures tied to savings, among them issues related to pension funds.
The tax on savings of less than 10 years' duration has been openly opposed by Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel and the powerful director-general of the prime minister's office, Avigdor Liberman.
Members of the committee that recommended the measures said on Sunday that without implementing the entire package, Israel's slumping stock and bond market had little prospect of recovery.
The committee was led by Finance Ministry Director-General David Brodett, who said he saw no alternative to the proposed measures.

"Failure to approve the Brodett Committee's measures will bring very negative results to the bourse, because it will appear that the government has no intention of dealing with the capital market's problem, the long-term problem, in a serious manner," committee member Amir Barnea told Israel Radio.
